note: The Garden's written questions. Every fact comes from the page named in src, read on that source's checked date. The first option is the right one; the app shuffles them. Brand questions are not here: garden.js builds them from brands.json.

PETA_LIST.t: PETA: Join the Ultimate Cruelty-Free List

PETA_VEGAN.t: PETA: Vegan companies that don't test

questions.q: "Cruelty-free" on a label is a promise about what?
questions.why: Cruelty-free is about testing: no new animal testing by the company or its suppliers.

questions.q: "Vegan" on a label is a promise about what?
options: The ingredients: nothing comes from an animal
questions.why: Vegan is about ingredients. It says nothing about testing.

questions.q: Can a product be vegan and still not be cruelty-free?
options: Yes, they are two separate things
questions.why: One is about ingredients, the other about testing. PETA says to look for both: cruelty-free and vegan.

questions.q: What does Leaping Bunny's certification cover?
questions.why: Leaping Bunny certifies testing. It does not certify that a product is vegan.

questions.q: How does Leaping Bunny say you can tell whether a product is vegan?
options: Read the ingredient list on the label
Look for the Leaping Bunny mark
questions.why: Leaping Bunny points to the ingredient list, which the law requires on the label.

questions.q: A cruelty-free promise is tied to a fixed cut-off date. Why a date?
options: Almost every ingredient was tested on animals at some point in the past
Certificates run out after one year
Laws differ from year to year
questions.why: So the promise is about the future: no new animal testing after the date.

questions.q: For a brand to be cruelty-free, who must not test on animals?
options: Only the stores that sell it
questions.why: Both programs look past the company to the suppliers of its ingredients.

questions.q: Where does PETA list companies that are both vegan and don't test?
options: On a separate list of vegan companies
On the same list, with no mark
questions.why: PETA keeps a separate list of vegan companies that don't test.

questions.q: PETA's list and Leaping Bunny's certification are:
options: The same program under two names
Both run by the U.S. government
questions.why: They are separate programs, so being on one says nothing about the other.

questions.q: Under Leaping Bunny, what does a company promise about its cut-off date?
options: No new animal testing after it, by itself or its suppliers
To be audited on that date
questions.why: The company picks a fixed cut-off date and commits to no new testing after it.

questions.q: How does a Leaping Bunny company keep track of its suppliers?
options: It collects written declarations from its manufacturers and suppliers
It tests samples in a lab
questions.why: This is Leaping Bunny's supplier monitoring system.

questions.q: How often does a Leaping Bunny company recommit?
questions.why: Leaping Bunny asks companies to recommit annually.

questions.q: A Leaping Bunny company must be open to what?
questions.why: Being open to an independent audit is part of the Standard.

questions.q: PETA's cruelty-free list has been running since:
questions.why: PETA dates its list of companies that don't test to 1987.

questions.q: What do companies on PETA's list verify?
options: That they and their suppliers never test on animals, now or in the future
That they are not sold online
That they passed a lab inspection
questions.why: The assurance covers the company and its suppliers, now and in the future.

questions.q: What did PETA start listing in 2018?
options: Individual brands that meet its rules across their whole product line
questions.why: Since October 2018 a brand can be listed on its own, if its whole line meets the rules.

questions.q: Can a certified cruelty-free brand be owned by a company that tests on animals?
options: Only if it is vegan too
questions.why: Leaping Bunny lists brands that were bought by parent companies it hasn't certified.

questions.q: When does Leaping Bunny keep a brand whose parent company tests?
options: Only if it runs as a stand-alone company with its own supply chain and still meets the Standard
Only if the parent pays a fee
questions.why: The brand has to operate on its own and keep meeting the Standard.

questions.q: What does Leaping Bunny say about shoppers and parent companies?
options: Many would rather not give money to a parent that hasn't committed to ending animal testing
Shoppers shouldn't look at who owns a brand
A parent company never affects a brand
Shoppers must write to the parent first
questions.why: Leaping Bunny notes that many shoppers prefer to avoid such parents, and leaves the choice to them.

questions.q: In C.F.B., a certified brand whose parent company tests shows as:
questions.why: Strict looks at the parent company. Certified looks only at PETA and Leaping Bunny.

questions.q: On Strict, a certified brand whose owner we couldn't confirm:
options: Passes, with a note that the parent isn't confirmed
Is marked as testing on animals
questions.why: Strict fails a brand only on a known problem with a source. An unknown passes with a note.

questions.q: Does selling in China automatically mean a brand tests on animals?
options: Not always: in specific cases a brand can sell there without animal testing
No, China has never asked for animal testing
questions.why: Leaping Bunny says changes to China's rules make it possible, under specific circumstances, to sell there and avoid animal testing. PETA still says products sold there are likely to be tested.

questions.q: What used to be true for brands importing makeup to sell in mainland China?
options: They had to test on animals
They had to sell online only
questions.why: Animal testing used to be required for imports sold in mainland China.

questions.q: Can a brand sell in mainland China and stay Leaping Bunny certified?
options: Yes, in specific cases, through Leaping Bunny's China program
Yes, any brand, with no checks
questions.why: Leaping Bunny runs a China program for the cases where the rules allow it.

questions.q: What does Leaping Bunny's China program do?
options: Checks the paperwork with regulatory experts and keeps watching after sales start
questions.why: It works with regulatory experts, reviews the documents and keeps monitoring.

questions.q: What does Leaping Bunny say about products sold to China online (cross-border e-commerce)?
options: It sees no animal testing for them
questions.why: Online cross-border sales are a different route from store shelves.

questions.q: Why does PETA ask companies that do business in China extra questions?
options: Products sold there are likely to be tested
questions.why: PETA treats selling in China as a reason to look closer.

questions.q: What does Leaping Bunny say about China's policies?
options: They have been the same for decades
questions.why: Leaping Bunny says it keeps a close watch on them.

questions.q: In C.F.B., what does Strict do with a brand known to be sold in mainland China stores?
options: It shows "Doesn't pass", with the source
questions.why: C.F.B. treats China store sales as a filter you choose, not as the meaning of cruelty-free.

questions.q: A brand isn't on PETA's list. Does that mean it tests on animals?
options: No. Missing from a list isn't proof
Yes, if it's a drugstore brand
questions.why: A company can be missing for other reasons.

questions.q: Which is a reason PETA gives for a company not being on its list?
options: It won't answer PETA's questions about its full policy
questions.why: PETA says a missing company likely won't respond to requests for its complete policy, or doesn't sell in an eligible region.

questions.q: PETA lists companies that sell in an "eligible region". Which regions does it name?
options: The U.S., Canada, India and Germany
questions.why: PETA says eligible regions include these four. A brand that doesn't sell in an eligible region may simply not be listed.

questions.q: What does C.F.B. show when it can't find proof either way?
questions.why: A missing listing is never treated as a yes or a no.
